strengths: Originality/significance: The paper explores a useful and apparently novel direction—using bidirectional Mamba-2 and Mamba–attention hybrids as masked-diffusion language-model denoisers. Demonstrating that attention is not essential for this setting could motivate more efficient diffusion-LM architectures.

Soundness positives: The experiments cover three nominal scales, two training-token budgets, validation perplexity, seven held-out perplexity datasets, several downstream benchmarks, and H100 latency/throughput measurements over a broad range of sequence lengths.

The long-sequence systems results are promising: pure Mamba variants retain substantially higher throughput than full attention as sequence length grows, while the hybrid generally provides the strongest reported language-modeling quality.

Presentation: The motivation, high-level architecture, and main empirical trends are easy to follow, and the paper appropriately describes its contribution as primarily architectural and empirical rather than algorithmic.
weaknesses: Soundness—decisive confound: the models are not parameter matched despite repeated claims of comparable budgets and an architecture-isolated evaluation. DiffuApriel has 0.29B versus 0.24B, 0.67B versus 0.52B, and 1.6B versus 1.3B parameters; the hybrids are also larger than their baselines. These differences reach roughly 25–30%, so the perplexity and downstream gains cannot be attributed reliably to the mixer architecture. Training tokens are held fixed, but training FLOPs are not reported or matched.

The efficiency evidence does not adequately substantiate the practical generation claims. Models are trained at context length 1,024, whereas the headline speedups occur at lengths up to 65,536 without any quality evaluation at those lengths. Figure 2 reports latency per forward pass, while Section 4.1 describes timing full 128-step decoding runs; it is unclear whether tokens/s denotes processed tokens, newly generated tokens, or end-to-end generation throughput. Sampling and host overheads are not broken out.

The claimed memory advantage is not measured, and the evaluation omits peak memory, maximum feasible batch size, end-to-end quality–latency curves, and comparisons across numbers of denoising steps. At the practically relevant trained context, the plots do not establish the same dramatic advantage as the 65K headline result.

There are no repeated training runs, uncertainty estimates, or statistical tests. This is especially problematic for the modest quality differences and downstream scores, several of which are near chance. The multiple-choice evaluation/scoring procedure for a diffusion model is not described sufficiently to validate these results.

Reproducibility is inadequate. The paper does not provide optimizer, learning-rate schedule, batch size, training steps, gradient clipping, initialization, hardware/training cost, precise noise-schedule parameters, checkpoint-selection protocol, code availability, or enough implementation detail for the bidirectional Mamba-2 block and CUDA-Graph benchmark. “Approximate Quokka optimal compute budget” is not an executable specification.

The method description is too schematic and at points technically misleading: Equations 4–6 present Mamba-2 as a simple linear recurrence with fixed kernel-shaped A/B quantities, omitting its input-dependent selective dynamics, projections, gates, convolution, state discretization, and bidirectional parameterization. The paper consequently does not specify precisely what was implemented or how timestep conditioning interacts with the actual Mamba-2 components.

Several quantitative and narrative errors weaken confidence. The reported reduction from 25.01 to 22.89 is about 8.5%, not “roughly 2%,” and 22.72 to 20.17 is about 11.2%. Table 3’s caption identifies DiffuApriel-H as best although DiffuApriel-H+MLP is best in every 1.3B column. Table 4 says the Mamba variants consistently outperform the baseline on all tasks, but DiffuApriel is worse on PIQA; descriptions of which architecture is strongest are also inconsistent.

Originality is meaningful but limited: the principal contribution is substituting/interleaving an established sequence mixer in an established masked-diffusion framework. There is little analysis explaining why bidirectional Mamba works as a denoiser, why K=5 is chosen, or how direction fusion and attention frequency affect quality and efficiency; key ablations are absent.

The limitations discussion is only a brief observation about short contexts and does not acknowledge the parameter/compute mismatch, evaluation ambiguity, absence of long-context quality tests, single-run evidence, or restriction to one dataset/tokenizer/hardware setup.

Research ethics are not discussed. Although no immediate high-risk intervention is introduced, a billion-parameter generative-model study should address DCLM data provenance/licensing and possible private or harmful content, bias and misuse, environmental/training cost, and whether generated outputs were safety-evaluated. Overall, the idea is promising, but the central quality and practical-efficiency claims need matched controls and a substantially more reproducible evaluation before acceptance.

strengths: The manuscript presents a clear and potentially useful architectural idea: applying bidirectional Mamba-2 mixers to masked diffusion language modeling, including both pure-SSM and attention/SSM hybrid variants.

The study compares several architectures at three nominal scales using the same dataset, tokenizer, diffusion objective, noise schedule, and 128-step sampler. Reporting validation likelihood, seven out-of-domain perplexity upper bounds, and downstream accuracy gives the empirical section reasonable breadth.

The efficiency measurements use a specified H100/bfloat16 setting, warm-ups, 20 decoding runs, and CUDA Graphs. The observed long-sequence scaling trend is qualitatively consistent with linear-complexity SSMs versus quadratic attention.

At the largest tested scale, the hybrid variants report consistently better likelihood and average downstream accuracy than the Transformer baseline, suggesting that the architectural direction merits further investigation.

The paper is organized around an understandable motivation and openly notes that its contribution is architectural and empirical rather than algorithmic. It also acknowledges that the efficiency advantage diminishes for short contexts. weaknesses: Soundness: the claimed controlled, parameter-matched comparison is not actually matched. DiffuTran has 0.24B/0.52B/1.3B parameters, whereas DiffuApriel has 0.29B/0.67B/1.6B and the hybrids 0.26B/0.61B/1.5B. These are differences of roughly 15–29%, while MLP widths also change across architectures. Equal token counts therefore do not establish equal training compute or isolate mixer choice, and no FLOP-matched or exactly parameter-matched comparison is provided.

Soundness: the headline efficiency result is measured primarily at lengths far outside the 1,024-token training context—up to 65,536 tokens—without any evaluation showing that model outputs remain meaningful at those lengths. Figure 2 appears to show little or no Mamba advantage around the trained context length, so the reported 4.4×–5.3× gains do not substantiate practical quality-matched generation speedups in the demonstrated operating regime.

Soundness: the efficiency protocol is internally ambiguous. Section 4.1 describes timings over full 128-step decoding runs, whereas Figure 2 labels latency as being per forward pass. It is unclear whether sampling, confidence calculation, token updates, synchronization, and other end-to-end costs are included. Raw timing values, memory use, uncertainty, software/kernel versions, and matched-quality speed comparisons are absent.

Soundness: the manuscript contains material numerical and interpretive errors. It describes reductions from 25.01 to 22.89 and from 22.72 to 20.17 as “roughly 2%,” although they are approximately 8.5% and 11.2%. It also says DiffuApriel-H is the best 1.3B zero-shot-perplexity model even though the table shows DiffuApriel-H+MLP winning every listed dataset. Such mistakes reduce confidence in the analysis.

The evidence does not support the broad generation claims. There is no direct generated-text evaluation, human assessment, diversity or degeneration analysis, infilling evaluation, or comparison of quality as the number of denoising steps changes. Perplexity upper bounds and mostly low multiple-choice accuracies alone do not establish that the proposed models provide a practical foundation for text generation.

No uncertainty is reported for training or evaluation: there are no independent seeds, standard deviations, confidence intervals, or significance tests. Several downstream differences are small, while the 1.3B scores are acknowledged to be modest, so claims of consistent superiority cannot be separated from run-to-run or evaluation variance.

Originality is moderate rather than high. The contribution mainly transfers an established bidirectional Mamba/hybrid-backbone recipe—already used in other sequence and diffusion domains—to masked text diffusion. There is little new algorithmic development or analysis of why the recurrence is particularly suitable for discrete denoising. The simplified recurrence equations also do not faithfully specify the selective Mamba-2 computation needed to reconstruct the model.

Important ablations are missing: there is no study of the attention interval K (fixed at 5), forward-only versus bidirectional SSMs, directional fusion, state size, alternative hybrid layouts, timestep conditioning, MLP allocation, or attention/SSM parameter allocation. Consequently, the claimed complementary roles of recurrence and attention are asserted from aggregate results rather than demonstrated.

The baseline coverage is narrow. Evaluation is limited to an in-house Transformer denoiser, with no empirical comparison against established diffusion LMs, block-diffusion or caching approaches, other efficient mixers, or autoregressive Mamba/Transformer systems. This makes both the absolute quality and practical significance difficult to judge.

Reproducibility is inadequate for the scale of the claims. The paper omits optimizer and learning-rate schedules, batch sizes, gradient settings, initialization, regularization, exact Chinchilla checkpoint/token budgets, total training compute and hardware, implementation or code availability, evaluation harness details, diffusion likelihood-estimation details, and exact sampling/scoring procedures for downstream tasks.

Presentation needs substantial revision. The prose repeatedly overstates what the experiments establish, terminology about Mamba capturing “local” dynamics versus attention supplying global context is insufficiently justified, the appendix largely duplicates the downstream discussion, and frequent spacing, grammar, capitalization, and cross-reference problems impede polish.

Limitations and ethics are underdeveloped. The limitations discussion is essentially one sentence about short contexts and does not address unmatched compute, extrapolation beyond the training length, weak absolute downstream performance, evaluation uncertainty, or the cost of 128 full-sequence passes. There is also no discussion of DCLM data provenance, bias, memorization, misuse, or the substantial compute/environmental footprint. These omissions are not themselves the decisive flaw, but they fall short of adequate responsible reporting.

strengths: The paper explores a timely and plausibly original direction: using bidirectional Mamba-2 and Mamba–attention hybrids as denoisers for masked diffusion language models. Demonstrating that attention is not essential for this setting is conceptually useful, even though the architectural ingredients themselves are established.

The controlled baseline is a meaningful strength: the proposed models and DiffuTran use the same data, tokenizer, diffusion objective, noise schedule, context length, and decoding-step count across three scales.

The empirical results are promising. At the largest scale, the hybrid-plus-MLP model improves validation perplexity under both compute budgets, wins all seven reported held-out perplexity evaluations, and raises average downstream accuracy from 33.81 to 38.24.

The throughput trends are convincing at a qualitative level and consistent with architectural complexity: pure Mamba remains efficient as sequence length grows, while the attention baseline deteriorates. The reported long-sequence gains are practically relevant for an iterative denoiser.

The manuscript is concise, well motivated, and generally easy to follow. It appropriately acknowledges that the advantages diminish at short context lengths and does not conceal that downstream absolute performance remains modest.
No immediate severe ethical concern is apparent; the work primarily studies model architecture and efficiency using established datasets.
weaknesses: The claimed controlled comparison is not actually parameter matched. DiffuApriel has 0.29B versus 0.24B parameters, 0.67B versus 0.52B, and 1.6B versus 1.3B—up to roughly 29% more parameters—while the paper labels these groups as 240M, 0.5B, and 1.3B. MLP widths also differ. This materially confounds both quality and throughput comparisons.

The efficiency evidence is narrower than the headline claims suggest. Figure 2 measures latency per model forward pass on synthetic lengths, rather than end-to-end generation latency or effective generated-token throughput. The models were trained only at length 1,024, whereas the largest speedups are reported at lengths up to 65,536, without demonstrating useful generation quality in that regime.

There are no uncertainty estimates, repeated-training runs, statistical tests, or error bars. Several quality differences are small, so it is unclear which gains exceed normal pretraining and evaluation variance.

Evaluation methodology is underspecified. The manuscript does not adequately explain how diffusion perplexity upper bounds or multiple-choice scores are computed, how prompts and answer choices are formatted, or whether likelihood normalization and benchmark harness settings are identical across architectures. This prevents reliable interpretation or replication of Tables 3 and 4.

Reproducibility is inadequate for the scale of the claims: optimizer settings, learning-rate schedules, batch sizes, training hardware, exact compute budgets, initialization, software versions, model implementation details, and code/checkpoint availability are absent. The simplified Mamba equations also do not specify the actual Mamba-2 block sufficiently to reconstruct it.

The experimental scope lacks comparisons to established diffusion-language-model systems, optimized diffusion caching methods, autoregressive Mamba/hybrid models, or standard efficient-attention baselines. Comparing only against an in-house Transformer denoiser makes it difficult to establish practical state-of-the-art significance.

The paper claims memory efficiency but reports no peak-memory measurements. It also gives no training-throughput, training-cost, FLOP, or quality-matched latency analysis, despite emphasizing efficiency and compute budgets.

Some empirical interpretations overreach the results. Pure DiffuApriel is often worse than DiffuTran at 240M and 0.5B, while the hybrid is generally strongest; consequently, the evidence supports the hybrid design more clearly than the broad claim that Mamba alone is a stronger denoising backbone.

There are reporting inconsistencies: the abstract highlights a 4.4× maximum, while Figure 2 reports 5.3× for one variant; the text calls a reduction from 25.01 to 22.89 “roughly 2%,” although it is about 8.5% relative; and Table 3's prose incorrectly identifies DiffuApriel-H rather than DiffuApriel-H+MLP as the best 1.3B model.

The limitations discussion is honest but too brief. It omits parameter-matching confounds, extrapolation far beyond training length, dependence on one GPU/software implementation, weak absolute downstream scores, lack of generation-quality evaluation, and possible data-governance or benchmark-contamination concerns associated with DCLM. These issues, particularly reproducibility and fairness of comparison, currently outweigh the promising idea.

strengths: Originality/significance: Applying bidirectional Mamba-2 mixers to masked diffusion language models is a useful and reasonably novel architectural direction. Demonstrating feasibility up to roughly 1.6B parameters is potentially valuable for efficient diffusion-based generation.

Soundness: The study includes Transformer, Mamba, and hybrid variants trained on the same dataset, tokenizer, context length, diffusion objective, and nominal token budgets. Evaluation covers validation and held-out perplexity, downstream accuracy, throughput, and latency.

Empirically, the hybrid model reports consistently favorable perplexity at the largest scale, while the pure Mamba model exhibits the expected superior long-sequence latency scaling. These results provide credible preliminary evidence that SSM denoisers deserve further study.

Presentation: The paper is generally readable and well organized, with useful throughput curves, a latency decomposition, architectural tables, and a concise limitations section. The authors appropriately acknowledge the lack of training for block-cached decoding and the batch-size-one evaluation.
The use of a single H100, warm-up iterations, repeated decoding runs, bf16, and CUDA graphs gives some useful context for the systems measurements.
weaknesses: Soundness: The claimed controlled, parameter-matched comparison is materially confounded. Table 5 compares 0.29B Mamba against 0.24B Transformer, 0.67B against 0.52B, and 1.6B against 1.3B; the hybrids are also larger. Nevertheless, the results tables relabel these as common 240M, 0.5B, and 1.3B scales. The largest Mamba models have roughly 15–29% more parameters, so their quality gains cannot be attributed cleanly to the mixer architecture.

The central quality–efficiency claim is not established. Throughput is measured with p in {8,16}, but no generation-quality results are reported at those denoising-step budgets. The limitations state that best quality occurs at p=1, making it especially important to show the degradation induced by the accelerated settings.

The strongest claimed inference method, block cache reuse, changes the bidirectional computation by restricting right-to-left updates to the current block and freezing prior representations. It is not the full-sequence denoiser used in training, and the paper provides no perplexity, downstream accuracy, or generation-quality evaluation under this altered algorithm. Raw throughput for a potentially degraded sampler is insufficient to establish superiority over AR or other DLM baselines.

The extreme-length measurements reach 65K–262K tokens although every model was trained with context length 1,024. No evidence shows that the models produce coherent or useful text at those lengths. Consequently, these experiments establish kernel/runtime scaling but not practically meaningful long-context generation.

Comparisons with the AR and Mamba-AR baselines are under-specified: their parameter counts, training data and compute, architectures, decoding setup, and output quality are not reported. Claims that block-cached DLMs outperform AR therefore lack a quality-matched and model-matched basis.

Reproducibility is inadequate for the scale of the claims. There is no code or checkpoint availability statement, and important details are missing or inconsistent: Table 6 gives one hidden dimension and layer count despite three scales; data subset construction, learning-rate warmup, training hardware and duration, random seeds, evaluation prompts and scoring, and implementation details for block caching are absent. No uncertainty is reported beyond stating that throughput averages five runs.

The architectural exposition is imprecise: Equations 4–6 and 7–9 describe fixed linear recurrences rather than the input-dependent selective dynamics, projections, gates, and convolutional components of Mamba-2. This makes it difficult to infer the implemented model from the manuscript.

Presentation contains consequential inaccuracies. For example, reducing perplexity from 22.72 to 20.17 is about 11%, not the stated 2%; the Chinchilla reduction from 25.01 to 22.89 is about 8.5%. Several broader conclusions—such as superior scaling of the inductive bias and strongest performance across all baselines—overstate what the confounded or quality-unmatched experiments demonstrate.

The paper provides no research-ethics or broader-impact discussion. Given the use of web-scale DCLM data and development of generative language models, data provenance, memorization, misuse, and bias considerations should at least be acknowledged. This is not by itself decisive, but it weakens the completeness of the submission.

strengths: Originality/significance: Applying a bidirectional Mamba-2 backbone to masked diffusion language modeling is a sensible and potentially useful direction. The pure-Mamba and interleaved-attention variants explore a relevant quality–efficiency trade-off.

The study spans three nominal model scales, two training-token regimes, several perplexity datasets, five downstream benchmarks, and multiple inference strategies. Training data, tokenizer, noise schedule, and token counts are held fixed within the reported comparisons.

The single-H100 measurements show a credible qualitative systems result: removing dense attention improves long-sequence scaling. The reported advantage reaches 8.2× over DiffuTran at 65K tokens, and the latency decomposition is directionally consistent with the expected linear versus quadratic sequence-mixing costs.

The paper is generally readable, includes asymptotic analysis and architectural details, and honestly acknowledges that block-cache-aware training, larger inference batches, and other step/acceptance settings remain unexplored.
weaknesses: Soundness: The central quality comparison is not controlled for model size or training compute. Models grouped as 240M, 0.5B, and 1.3B actually contain 0.24B versus 0.29B/0.26B, 0.52B versus 0.67B/0.61B, and 1.3B versus 1.6B/1.5B parameters, respectively. Thus the Mamba models are up to about 29% larger and consume more training compute at the same token count. This substantially confounds the claimed architectural superiority, especially the modest downstream and perplexity gains.

The headline throughput results are not paired with generation-quality measurements at the evaluated decoding settings. The models are trained with context length 1,024 but benchmarked at lengths up to 65K or 262K, and block caching changes the bidirectional computation by restricting right-to-left updates to the current block. No perplexity, accuracy, coherence, or equivalence test establishes that outputs in these extreme-length and accelerated regimes remain useful. Consequently, the paper demonstrates raw execution speed, not a validated quality–throughput advantage.

Comparisons with autoregressive models in Figures 2c–d are especially under-supported. Diffusion uses assumed fixed step factors p=8 or 16, while the paper itself states that best quality occurs at p=1. Without quality-matched decoding, the claim that block-cached DLMs outperform AR baselines is not meaningful. The AR baselines and their training/configuration are also insufficiently documented.

The evaluation lacks statistical support: training seeds, variation across runs, confidence intervals, and uncertainty for the latency fits are absent. Throughput averages only five decoding runs, and Figure 3 reports neither fitted coefficients nor goodness of fit. There are also no ablations of attention frequency N=5, bidirectionality, fusion choice, or parameter matching.

Reproducibility is inadequate. No code or model-release commitment is provided; preprocessing, training duration/steps, hardware for training, software and kernel versions, evaluation prompts, multiple-choice scoring, and perplexity-upper-bound implementation are unspecified. Table 6 further conflicts with Table 5 by listing a universal hidden dimension of 960, 24 blocks, and 24 heads even though Table 5 includes dimension 1,920 and 36-layer configurations.

Presentation contains misleading or inconsistent claims. The paper repeatedly calls the parameter budgets comparable and says the mixer is the only difference despite the sizeable parameter discrepancies. It describes 25.01 to 22.89 and 22.72 to 20.17 as roughly a 2% reduction, although these are 2.12/2.55 absolute points and approximately 8.5%/11.2% relative reductions. It also sometimes conflates throughput with overall “performance.”

Originality is moderate rather than high: replacing attention with bidirectional Mamba and using a standard Mamba–attention hybrid are natural transfers of established designs. The work provides limited new methodological insight beyond this substitution, and the simplified recurrence equations do not faithfully specify the input-dependent Mamba-2 mechanism.

The limitations section is candid but incomplete. It does not recognize the parameter/compute confound, absence of long-context quality evaluation, or lack of quality-matched AR comparisons. There is also no discussion of data bias, misuse, or training energy. The work introduces no obvious unusual ethical risk, but its research-ethics and resource reporting are thin. Overall, the core efficiency direction is promising, but important evidential and reproducibility deficiencies prevent acceptance in the present form.

strengths: Originality/significance: The paper explores a timely and useful architectural intersection—bidirectional Mamba-2 denoisers for masked diffusion language models—and appears to be the first systematic study of this combination for text at scales up to roughly 1.5–1.6B parameters.

Soundness: Comparing pure-attention, pure-Mamba, and hybrid models under the same dataset, tokenizer, diffusion objective, noise schedule, context length, and token budget isolates several important architectural factors. Results across validation perplexity, seven held-out corpora, and five downstream tasks consistently suggest that Mamba-based denoisers are viable.

The hybrid model produces encouraging modeling results at the largest scale, outperforming the Transformer baseline on every reported held-out perplexity dataset. The pure-Mamba model also performs competitively, supporting the core feasibility claim independently of the hybrid.

The empirical systems study spans multiple decoding schemes and unusually long benchmark lengths. The observed scaling trends are qualitatively consistent with the expected linear versus quadratic sequence-mixing costs, and the latency decomposition helps explain the throughput curves.

Presentation is generally clear and well organized. The paper distinguishes modeling quality from systems performance, includes architecture and hyperparameter tables, and candidly identifies fixed acceptance assumptions, batch-size-one testing, and the absence of block-cache-aware training as limitations.
weaknesses: The central comparison is not parameter controlled despite repeated claims of comparable budgets and architecture-isolated evaluation. Table 5 compares 0.24B/0.52B/1.3B Transformers with 0.29B/0.67B/1.6B pure-Mamba models and 0.26B/0.61B/1.5B hybrids—up to about 29% more parameters. Thus, the reported quality improvements do not establish that Mamba is superior at matched capacity; matched-parameter or matched-training-FLOP controls are needed.

The strongest efficiency claim is not paired with generation quality. Models are trained only at context length 1,024, yet throughput is benchmarked to 65K or 262K tokens without evidence that outputs at those lengths are coherent. Likewise, block-cache decoding freezes past representations and restricts the reverse Mamba pass within a block, but the paper reports no perplexity or generation-quality degradation from this approximation. Consequently, outperforming autoregressive models in tokens/second does not establish a useful quality-matched speed advantage.

The decoding-step choice K=L/p assumes fixed multi-token progress for p in {8,16}. The limitations acknowledge that best quality occurs near p=1, but no quality–latency curve, realized acceptance statistics, or matched-quality operating point is reported. Headline speedups such as 8.2× and the claim that block-cached DLMs are faster than AR therefore depend on an unvalidated quality assumption.

Several quantitative statements are inaccurate or ambiguous. For example, Table 2 describes 22.89 versus 25.01 (and 20.17 versus 22.72) as roughly a 2% perplexity reduction, although the relative reductions are approximately 8.5% and 11.2%. Figure 2/text also inconsistently associates the 8.2× result with K=L/8 versus K=L/16. Such errors weaken confidence in the empirical interpretation.

Theoretical and architectural exposition is too simplified for reproducibility. Equations 4–6/7–9 describe fixed linear recurrences rather than the input-dependent selective dynamics, gating, projections, convolution, and discretization of Mamba-2. The asymptotic table is asserted without a derivation and mixes compute-, memory-, and peak-throughput regimes in ways that make some formulas and comparisons difficult to audit.

Evaluation reporting is incomplete: there are no seeds, confidence intervals, training curves, estimator details for diffusion perplexity upper bounds, downstream prompting/scoring protocols, or ablations over bidirectionality, attention frequency N, state size, and parameter matching. The downstream scores are also low enough that uncertainty and chance-level context matter.

Reproducibility is only partial. The manuscript gives useful high-level hyperparameters and hardware, but provides no code, checkpoints, exact data preprocessing, optimizer implementation details, software/kernel versions, total training compute, or scripts for the custom block-cache benchmark. Table 6 additionally lists a single hidden size and block count that do not describe all scales without consulting Table 5.

Research ethics and broader impacts are not discussed. Although the work presents no unusual immediate ethical hazard, training generative models on DCLM raises standard questions about data provenance, privacy, bias, misuse, and energy consumption that should be acknowledged. Overall, the promising core idea merits further development, but the unmatched model sizes and absence of quality-matched long-context decoding evidence leave the headline claims insufficiently supported for acceptance in the current form.
